newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-ISI opposes rushed decision on NZ super.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-ISI opposes rushed decision on NZ super.

text.p: Policy decisions on New Zealand superannuation arrived at during coalition negotiations could be premature and harmful, the Investment Savings and Insurance Association said on Tuesday.
Chief executive Roger Gill said far more transparent and fuller debate was needed before political parties began examining the merits of voluntary versus compulsory pension schemes.

"All the indications are that there is a danger of some sort of commitment to a compulsory regime being made behind closed doors, without the issues actually being talked through and thought through properly," Gill said in an interview.

"We think before you talk about compulsory or voluntary or any sort of variation, it's important, in fact it's essential, that there is a commitment from all parliamentary parties to agree...that there needs to be a long term, stable policy on retirement saving and on saving generally."
New Zealand First, which wants a compulsory savings scheme, currently holds the balance of power and is negotiating with both the caretaker National Party government and Labour.
Gill said it was "terribly important" that superannuation was not merely a small part of a coalition deal designed to get a particular government into power.
"It's got to be wider. It really has to go right across the political party spectrum, and there needs to be as much agreement as possible," he said.

"I wouldn't think for one minute you'll get all the political parties agreeing on everything, but this is just too important to become a political football, to remain a political football as it has been."
Gill said it was essential the broad thrust of superannuation policy could remain intact through another potential change in government.
"If it's something that's cropping up every three years, then you're going to have uncertainty and instability and you won't be able to encourage savings," he said.

He said the ISI did not have an official position on whether voluntary or compulsory superannuation was better. But he said it was interesting that both National and Labour had made strong public comments against a compulsory regime.
It would be premature for a coalition deal to include a move to compulsory superannuation, he said.

"There are too many aspects of the compulsory side that need to be thought through. It's a bit like saying we think it should be compulsory, now we're going to sort out how we're going to do it. That doesn't give anybody any confidence to save at all."

Gill pointed out that New Zealand First, the only major party with compulsory saving as part of its election platform, received only 13 percent of the party vote. He said the ISI wanted the review of the multi-party accord on superannuation, scheduled for late next year, to be brought forward as a matter of urgency.
"If these things are being talked about now, bring forward the review. There is a wide range of views out there on the issue, and it's important those views are aired."
